[/page/5/Text/2] Therefore, in this study we interviewed survivors of medically serious 'near-lethal' suicide attempts, an approach that appears to provide a valid proxy for completed suicide (Douglas et al., 2004).

The first author, Adrienne Rivlin (AR), conducted face-to-face interviews with participants in private, after obtaining informed consent. The interviews lasted between 30 and 120 minutes. To collect information on the suicidal process we used a semi-structured qualitative interview schedule.
[/page/7/Text/7] Between 1 June 2007 and 6 February 2009 we interviewed 60 male prisoners from 19 prisons who had made near-lethal suicide attempts.

evidence.section_title: The suicidal process in male prisoners making near-lethal suicide attempts
evidence.quote: The suicide attempts often followed adverse life events (especially broken relationships or bereavement), criminal justice/prison-related factors (e.g. concerns about sentencing) and psychiatric or psychological factors (e.g. drug/alcohol withdrawal, depression/anxiety and hearing voices). The suicidal process in prisoners is a complex interplay of background factors, adverse life events, mental health and psychological problems and cognitive processes. Half the prisoners believed their acts could have been prevented, often with relatively simple solutions.

Approximately one-third of prisoners had explicitly told someone (for example, a family member or psychiatrist) of their wish to die. Two (3%) prisoners said that they had made ambiguous references to family that they might take their own lives. Table 3. Categories of images reported during the near-lethal suicide attempts. Image of/that... Yourself planning/preparing to harm yourself or make a suicide attempt. The things you were escaping from by attempting suicide. What might happen to you if you died. What might happen to other people if you died. A real event that happened to you (e.g. a traumatic event but not suicide or self-harm). A memory of a time you tried to harm yourself in the past. Made you feel safe or better. 'I saw a picture of my father and mother'. (Case 51)

[/page/14/Text/15] Over half the prisoners (27/46, 59%) said that they chose not to tell anyone outside prison about their attempted suicide. This was usually because there was either no one to tell or they did not want to upset or worry their family: [/page/15/Text/3] I try and keep it as quiet as possible cause I don't want to get bullied ... people will think you can't cope or something. (Case 1) [/page/15/Text/9] Conversely, some prisoners also expressed a desire to attempt suicide again: [/page/15/Text/10] It [the suicide attempt] don't affect me. I'd do it again. I'd say give me a gun now and I'll blow me head off. That's it. (Case 23) [/page/14/Text/17] When prisoners' families and friends did find out about the suicide attempt, prisoners said that the predominant reaction was one of upset or concern for the prisoner. Similarly, prisoners said that the reactions they faced from inside the prison following a suicide attempt were largely positive. Most prisoners felt that they were treated better, 'OK' or no differently by staff. [/page/15/Text/7] Another common feeling was that the suicide attempt had made the prisoner feel better than before the act: [/page/15/Text/8] It was a slap round the face with reality. It made me feel much better. I've had a think about things and realised that I am a silly little arse and that there is more than just my feelings. (Case 28)

evidence.section_title: Could the act have been prevented?
evidence.quote: [/page/16/Text/7] Half the prisoners (21/42, 50%) believed that their act could have been prevented. Sometimes they thought this could have been achieved with a relatively easy solution, for example, a phone call, receiving necessary medication or being in a double cell: [/page/16/Text/8] Giving me my medication to make me feel normal. Then I would have been right as rain. I am back to normal now. I am okay now. (Case 33) [/page/16/Text/9] Whilst 2/42 (5%) prisoners were unsure about whether their act could have been prevented, 19/42 (45%) prisoners did not think the suicide attempt could have been stopped under any circumstances:
